name: Phyllodes tumour of the breast
aliases: benign, borderline and malignant phyllodes tumour

clinicalPearls: A fibroepithelial neoplasm of the breast in which the stromal (mesenchymal) component drives the tumour, forming characteristic leaf-like (phyllodes) fronds projecting into cystic spaces
Classified into a spectrum of benign, borderline and malignant grades based on stromal cellularity, atypia, mitotic activity, margin appearance and stromal overgrowth
Typically presents in middle-aged women as a firm, rapidly enlarging, painless breast mass, often larger than a fibroadenoma
Distinguishing benign phyllodes tumour from a cellular fibroadenoma can be difficult, and core biopsy may not reliably separate them
Stromal overgrowth, defined as stroma without accompanying epithelium in a low-power field, is an important adverse feature
MED12 mutations are shared with fibroadenoma, while progression to higher grade is associated with additional alterations such as TERT promoter mutations and other tumour-suppressor changes
Wide local excision with an adequate rim of normal tissue is the goal; axillary dissection is not required because malignant tumours spread haematogenously, not typically to nodes
reference.pathophysiology: Phyllodes tumours are biphasic fibroepithelial lesions in which the neoplastic stroma is the driving component, producing exaggerated leaf-like architecture and, in higher grades, sarcomatous features. Early tumours often share MED12 mutations with fibroadenomas, indicating a common starting point, whereas progression towards borderline and malignant grades accumulates further genetic alterations, including TERT promoter mutations and loss of tumour-suppressor function, that increase stromal cellularity, atypia and proliferation. Malignant tumours can undergo heterologous sarcomatous differentiation and metastasise through the bloodstream rather than via lymphatics.
additionalDifferentials: Fibroadenoma, especially the cellular and juvenile variants
Metaplastic (spindle cell) carcinoma of the breast
Malignant heterologous elements mimicking a separate sarcoma
additionalInvestigations: Triple assessment with clinical examination, breast imaging and biopsy
Core-needle biopsy, recognising its limitations in separating phyllodes tumour from cellular fibroadenoma
Histological grading assessing stromal cellularity, atypia, mitoses, margins and stromal overgrowth
Breast ultrasound and mammography, with MRI when extent is unclear
Staging imaging for distant (haematogenous) metastasis in malignant tumours
Molecular studies (for example MED12 and TERT promoter status) in selected diagnostically difficult cases
redFlags: Rapid increase in size of a breast mass
Malignant-grade histology with marked stromal overgrowth, atypia and high mitotic activity
Positive or close excision margins predicting local recurrence
Signs of haematogenous metastasis, particularly to the lungs
Heterologous sarcomatous differentiation within the tumour
reference.prognosis: Benign phyllodes tumours have an excellent prognosis when completely excised, with recurrence linked mainly to inadequate margins; borderline tumours recur more often, and malignant phyllodes tumours can metastasise haematogenously, most commonly to the lungs, carrying a significantly worse outlook, so wide excision with clear margins is the key determinant of local control across all grades.
pitfalls: Diagnosing a cellular fibroadenoma on core biopsy and missing a phyllodes tumour
Performing axillary lymph node dissection, which is unnecessary given haematogenous spread
Excising with inadequate margins, leading to local recurrence
Overlooking stromal overgrowth or heterologous sarcomatous elements when grading
Underestimating recurrence risk in borderline tumours treated as clearly benign
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Breast Tumours
WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours
management: Grade phyllodes tumours as benign, borderline, or malignant based on margin character, atypia, mitotic activity, and stromal overgrowth, ideally reviewed by a breast or soft-tissue pathologist, and let grade drive management.
Local excision to negative margins is the mainstay of treatment across the entire grade spectrum, not just for benign disease, whenever an adequate cosmetic result can be achieved.
Reserve mastectomy for tumours too large relative to the breast to allow adequate excision with acceptable cosmesis, rather than defaulting to it for malignant grade.
Avoid enucleation since shelling out the tumour without a margin raises the risk of local recurrence, and re-excise any inadequate or positive margins.

A margin width of at least 2 mm has not been shown to reduce local recurrence compared with a narrower clear margin in contemporary series, so the traditional wide-clear-margin mandate can be revisited rather than pursuing very wide excision at the cost of cosmesis.
Do not perform axillary lymph node dissection or routine axillary staging, since nodal metastases are rare; pursue axillary surgery only if clinically suspicious nodes are present.

Consider adjuvant radiotherapy with wide excision for borderline or malignant phyllodes tumours, particularly when margins are close and further re-excision is not feasible, recognizing this role is not firmly established and radiotherapy is not used for benign lesions.
Systemic therapy is not part of routine management of localized phyllodes tumour and should be considered mainly for unresectable, extensive, or metastatic malignant disease.

When systemic therapy is used for malignant phyllodes tumour, follow soft-tissue sarcoma-directed approaches such as anthracycline-based or other sarcoma regimens rather than epithelial breast cancer regimens, since no specific regimen is established as standard for this entity.

Because metastatic spread is haematogenous rather than lymphatic and the lung is the dominant site of distant relapse, use chest imaging for staging and surveillance in borderline or malignant disease rather than routine axillary imaging.
Follow all patients with regular clinical breast examination and breast imaging to detect local recurrence.

Refer any core-biopsy result that is difficult to distinguish from a cellular fibroadenoma, or any rapidly enlarging breast mass, for surgical or breast-specialist evaluation and excisional confirmation rather than reassurance from core biopsy alone.

Manage borderline or malignant grade, close or positive margins, or cases requiring sarcoma-type systemic therapy through a breast multidisciplinary team with specialist pathology review, involving sarcoma-service input when systemic therapy is being considered.
